Gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus) females produce an average of four pups per litter [N_R_i = four pups per litter] and typically raise a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], a reproductive strategy that reflects their solitary, territorial lifestyle across diverse North American habitats. Under the thermal conditions typical of this species' active metabolic state of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], gestation proceeds over a period of approximately 57 days [tg = approximately 57 days], a duration consistent with other mid-sized canids. Neonates are born in dense brush or rocky dens following this gestation interval, emerging as altricial, blind pups entirely dependent on maternal care. The reproductive output per year is modest compared to canids that produce larger litters or multiple litters annually, reflecting the gray fox's reliance on stable, defended resources rather than high-turnover reproductive strategies. Field observations from radio-tracking studies across the southeastern United States indicate that den site selection, often in hollow logs or crevices, is critical for neonatal survival during the first weeks of life.

Newborn gray foxes emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 94 grams [Wwb = approximately 94 grams], a neonatal mass that places them within the typical range for canids of this body size. This initial mass underscores the altricial nature of the pups at parturition, as they lack both thermoregulatory capacity and locomotor ability for the first several days. The period of lactation and maternal dependence extends for roughly 55 days since birth [tx = roughly 55 days since birth] under the same thermal conditions of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C] in which gestation unfolded. During this interval, pups transition from exclusive milk ingestion to the consumption of solid food items, including small mammals, fruits, and insects brought to the den by both parents. By the time of weaning, the offspring have achieved a wet weight at weaning of 519.7 grams [Wwx = 519.7 grams], representing a more than fivefold increase from birth mass that reflects the high energetic investment provided through maternal lactation and biparental provisioning. The weaning weight is a key indicator of the nutritional quality of the maternal territory.

Following the transition to nutritional independence, juvenile gray foxes continue to develop within their natal territory, refining hunting skills through play and observational learning. The attainment of sexual maturity occurs relatively late in this species, with individuals reaching puberty at 345 days after birth [tp = 345 days after birth] when maintained at the species' normal core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This extended juvenile period, lasting nearly a full year, is notably longer than that observed in red foxes (Vulpes vulpes) or coyotes (Canis latrans) of comparable body size, suggesting a slower life-history pace in Urocyon cinereoargenteus. The delayed onset of gonadal activity is likely linked to the species' reliance on stable territories and the need for advanced cognitive and motor skills required for successful independent foraging in complex woodland environments. Sub-adults may disperse considerable distances, up to several tens of kilometers, in search of unoccupied habitat, a behavior that carries substantial mortality risk during the first post-dispersal winter.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females is approximately 4750 grams [Wwi = approximately 4750 grams], a mass that reflects the energetic equilibrium of a long-lived, solitary carnivore and forms the basis for comparison across North American canids. Though some sources report that larger individuals may reach as much as 9 kilograms, reflecting considerable geographic and seasonal variation in body condition, this adult mass is intermediate among North American canids, placing the gray fox below the red fox and coyote but above the kit fox (Vulpes macrotis) and swift fox (Vulpes velox). Males tend to be slightly heavier than females, a pattern of sexual size dimorphism typical of canids that engage in territorial defense. The species' slender build and relatively long tail, traits that facilitate agile climbing behavior unique among canids, are supported by this moderate body mass. Comparative studies of mass across the genus Urocyon show that the island fox (Urocyon littoralis) is substantially smaller, with adult masses averaging less than 2 kilograms, suggesting that body size in this lineage is evolutionarily labile in response to insular versus mainland ecological pressures.

Lifespan in the gray fox, measured under field conditions at the species' normal active body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], averages approximately 16.2 years [am = approximately 16.2 years], a remarkable longevity for a canid of this body size. This extended lifespan is comparable to that of captive red foxes and exceeds that reported for most wild canid populations, where predation, disease, and anthropogenic mortality typically reduce survival. The annual reproductive output of approximately four pups per year reflects the species' position on the slow end of the canid life-history continuum, where high adult survival buffers low fecundity. Factors contributing to this delayed senescence include the species' relatively low basal metabolic rate, its ability to exploit diverse dietary resources from small vertebrates to persimmons and berries, and its cryptic, arboreal escape behavior that reduces predation risk. Population modeling suggests that adult survival, rather than fecundity, is the primary driver of population growth in this species, underscoring the importance of preserving habitat connectivity for long-lived territorial carnivores.
